(This evening through Sunday)...
Issued at 130 PM EST Sun Nov 1 2026

Overview.

A quiet start to the week will give way to an active and 
significantly warmer pattern by Tuesday. Sprinkles and light rain 
showers will continue intermittently through tomorrow. As high 
pressure shifts eastward, much warmer air will surge north into the 
region Tuesday. A strong low pressure system will track across the 
Midwest on Tuesday night, bringing widespread rain, gusty winds, and 
the potential for a few thunderstorms. Behind this system, much 
colder and drier air will sweep in for Thursday with temperatures 
closer to normal through the weekend.

Tonight through Monday Night.

Surface high pressure centered across the upper Ohio Valley and 
central Appalachians will continue shifting east off the Mid-
Atlantic coast tonight. Aloft, quasi-zonal flow transitions to weak 
southwesterly flow downstream of an upper-level shortwave crossing 
the Upper Mississippi Valley. Warm air advection intensifies across 
the lower Ohio Valley after midnight as an 850mb low-level jet ramps 
up to 25 to 35 kt. Additional saturation in the lower levels is 
expected to continue through the overnight with saturation currently 
at around 700mb which should then saturate to near the surface by 
Monday morning. The cloud deck should be shallow by Monday morning 
which will increase the chance that the weak isentropic lift could 
bring precipitation to the surface.

Scattered showers will continue across the forecast area through 
Monday morning before large-scale isentropic ascent shifts eastward 
into Ohio by early afternoon. A weak, diffuse surface warm front 
will attempt to advance northward toward the Ohio River, but 
persistent overcast conditions, weak low-level easterly to 
southeasterly flow, and rain-cooled air will reinforce a wedge of 
cooler air across central Indiana. This will limit daytime 
insolation, keeping afternoon temperatures capped in the mid-50s 
north to lower 60s south.  For Monday night, mid-level forcing 
diminishes behind the departing northern-stream impulse. However, 
residual boundary-layer moisture beneath a low-level inversion 
around 900mb will maintain widespread stratus and the potential for 
some drizzle. Weak warm advection continues just above the surface, 
keeping overnight lows mild and well above seasonal normals, 
generally settling in the upper 40s to lower 50s.

Tuesday through Sunday.

Tuesday will initially feature a brief synoptic lull as an expansive 
upper-level ridge axis temporarily builds over the eastern third of 
the CONUS in response to a deep, amplifying longwave trough over the 
western United States. Central Indiana will reside firmly within the 
warm sector as the surface warm front lifts north into the lower 
Great Lakes. Southerly boundary-layer flow will transport 850mb 
temperatures of +10C to +12C into the region, pushing surface highs 
into the mid to upper 70s. Aside from isolated showers driven by 
weak warm advection, large-scale subsidence should keep the majority 
of the daylight hours dry beneath broken cloud cover.

The primary focus centers on the evening and overnight hours as 
the western trough rounds its base, acquires a neutral to slightly
negative tilt, and ejects into the Mid- Mississippi Valley. 
Deterministic solutions from the GFS, ECMWF, along with their 
respective ensembles, remain in good agreement regarding a rapidly
deepening surface cyclone tracking from northern Missouri 
northeastward across Illinois into the western Great Lakes. 
Kinematic fields associated with this system are exceptionally 
potent. An intense 850mb LLJ of 55 to 65 kt will overspread 
Indiana Wednesday afternoon and evening, accompanied by a 90 to 
100 kt mid- level jet streak overhead. Bulk shear vectors in the 
0-6 km layer will exceed 60 to 70 kt, oriented largely parallel to
the advancing surface cold front, while 0-1 km bulk shear climbs 
to 35 to 45 kt.

All these favorable dynamics will be countered by an increasingly 
hostile thermodynamic field with very poor lapse rates and little to 
no instability. Model soundings show little to no instability except 
for the far southwestern counties and with the poor timing of an 
overnight passage of the front, severe weather looks increasingly 
unlikely with a HSLC event not really in play anymore. Models have a 
much better handle on the timing with little difference in the 
ensembles which boosts confidence in the decreased severe threat. 
Outside of the rain chances, the strong low level wind fields will 
help to bring breezy conditions with a few gusts up to 30 mph at 
times. There may be a few showers that linger into Wednesday, but 
expect chances to fall off quickly as slightly cooler air works into 
the area.
